<reason>Both sides were strong, compliant with format, and adapted across rounds. A's best live route was incidence: the hospital concession ("the public purse pays it") framed as a spending program smuggled through labor law, plus the "statute can coordinate a worse equilibrium" reply. But B answered the hospital pressure honestly and substantively — the burnout/attrition budget, the weekend/holiday precedent that societies deliberately buy rest — and A never engaged that analogy. On the alternatives clash, B's closing was decisive: A's overtime-threshold substitute drops the pay-protection clause, meaning workers who get a shorter week buy it out of their own wages, which concedes away the motion's core benefit. B also survived the coordination exchange: A's "statute is needed only where the math fails" was squarely answered by the externality point (private math fails because firms don't capture public gains), and A's closing did not re-engage. A's clipped turns (opening and rebuttal 2) cost some development. B made the debate marginally easier to decide and closed the two most important pressures cleaner.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The hospital funding exchange: A's Q1 forced B to name who pays; B conceded "the public purse" but reframed it as converting unbudgeted attrition costs into budgeted staffing, invoking the weekend precedent — and then A's Q2/Rebuttal 2 "statute is needed only where the math fails" was answered by B's externality argument (Ford precedent, uncaptured public gains), which A never rebutted. The parallel clash over A's alternative ending in B's closing "buy it out of her own wages" was the sharpest single blow.</best_rebuttal>
